# Things to watch

Short videos, for when reading is not landing.

Watching is good for the **feel** of a tool: where somebody's mouse goes, how
fast it is, what it looks like when it works. It is not a substitute for the
step by step pages here, because those are written for *your* project with
*your* component names in them. Use both.

You can pause a video. You can watch it twice. Nobody is timing you.

> **If a link is dead, search the title.** Videos get taken down and pages get
> moved. Tell your teacher and we will swap it for a better one.

---

## Writing user stories

Start here if you are stuck on acceptance criteria, which is where most people
get stuck.

| Watch | Why |
|---|---|
| [What Are User Story Acceptance Criteria?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DavPyEFeEFw) | The clearest short explanation of what a criterion actually is |
| [User Stories and Acceptance Criteria EXAMPLE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q26147zlcMU) | Somebody working through a real one, start to finish |

**Then read:** [Writing a user story](/build/writing-a-story.html), and open
[the story studio](/trail-crew/write).

## A word about watching versus doing

It is genuinely possible to watch six hours of tutorials and be no better at
this than when you started. It feels like learning because it is somebody
competent doing the thing, and watching somebody competent is pleasant.

The rule that works: **watch a video once, then go and do the thing badly.**
Being stuck for ten minutes on your own app teaches you more than another hour
of somebody else's. Then, when you are stuck on something specific, come back
and watch the ten seconds that covers it.

That is also why every page here is written for your project rather than a
generic one. A tutorial shows somebody else's app. Your architecture page has
your button names on it.
